title: Exam-Style
explanation_style: Binomial-depth tutoring (Ch13): shared solution_overview; each letter teaches the idea, derives step by step on the given numbers/figure, explains traps, closes naturally with True/False.

tasks.title: Carpentry workshop: revenue, cost, and build time
tasks.context:
A small carpentry workshop builds and sells wooden chairs. Let $Q$ be the number of chairs (treated as continuous). Revenue in euros is $R(Q)=-3Q^{2}+90Q$. Production cost in euros is $C(Q)=0.5Q^{3}-9Q^{2}+60Q+200$. After an assembly-bench reconfiguration the build-time function (hours) is
$$T(Q)=\begin{cases}0.5Q^{2}+4Q & \text{if }Q<12\\ 12Q-24 & \text{if }Q\ge 12.\end{cases}$$
The owner is comparing operating decisions, average-cost movements, and a nearby rival rather than looking at any one formula in isolation. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Profit (revenue minus cost) reaches its highest value when $Q=15$ chairs are made and sold.
Starting from an output of $Q_{0}$ chairs, building one extra chair changes the average cost per chair by roughly $Q_{0}-9-\dfrac{200}{Q_{0}^{2}}$.
The build-time function $T(Q)$ rises more steeply at $Q=11$ than at $Q=15$.

A rival workshop's revenue $R_{e}(Q)$ satisfies $R_{e}(6)=R(6)$, and its marginal revenue exceeds this workshop's, $R_{e}^{\prime}(Q)>R^{\prime}(Q)$, throughout $6\le Q\le 10$. It then follows that $R_{e}(9)<R(9)$.
Revenue is largest at an output exceeding $12$ chairs.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Profit is revenue minus cost. An interior peak requires $P^{\prime}=0$ with the right sign pattern — guessing $Q=15$ from the revenue schedule is the trap here.

Profit is revenue minus cost, so form $P=R-C$ and look for where its derivative vanishes.

$$
P(Q) = -0.5Q^{3}+6Q^{2}+30Q-200
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -1.5Q^{2}+12Q+30
$$

Factoring gives

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -1.5(Q-10)(Q+2)
$$

The only positive critical point is $Q=10$, and at $Q=15$ one already has $P^{\prime}(15)<0$, so profit is falling there rather than peaking.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

The one-unit change in average cost is the derivative of $AC=C/Q$, not the derivative of total cost. Divide first, then differentiate.

Average cost is total cost per chair, so divide $C$ by $Q$ before differentiating.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}
$$

$$
= 0.5Q^{2}-9Q+60+\dfrac{200}{Q}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = Q-9-\dfrac{200}{Q^{2}}
$$

Starting from output $Q_{0}$, the change in average cost from one extra chair is approximated by that derivative evaluated at $Q_{0}$, which is exactly the expression in the claim.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Steepness means the local slope $T^{\prime}$ on the active branch. The kink at $Q=12$ forces different formulas at $Q=11$ and $Q=15$.

Steepness of build time is the derivative of whichever branch is active at the stated output.

On $Q<12$,

$$
T^{\prime}(Q) = Q+4
$$

$$
T^{\prime}(11) = 15
$$

On $Q\ge 12$,

$$
T^{\prime}(Q) = 12
$$

$$
T^{\prime}(15) = 12
$$

Since $15>12$, build time rises more steeply at $Q=11$ than at $Q=15$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Equal starting revenue plus a strict marginal-revenue advantage integrates to a larger ending revenue. The claim asserts the opposite inequality.

The rival starts at the same revenue at $Q=6$ but has strictly larger marginal revenue on the way to $Q=9$, so integrate that inequality.

$$
R_{e}(9)-R_{e}(6)>R(9)-R(6)
$$

With $R_{e}(6)=R(6)$, this forces

$$
R_{e}(9)>R(9)
$$

The claim asserts the opposite inequality.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Revenue peaks where $R^{\prime}=0$ and $R^{\prime\prime}<0$ — a different first-order condition from the profit peak at $Q=10$.

Revenue peaks where marginal revenue is zero and the second derivative is negative.

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = -6Q+90
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 0
$$

$$
Q = 15
$$

$$
R^{\prime\prime}(Q) = -6<0
$$

That critical output $15$ exceeds $12$, so revenue is largest beyond twelve chairs.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Revenue is $R(Q)=-3Q^{2}+90Q$ and cost is $C(Q)=0.5Q^{3}-9Q^{2}+60Q+200$. Profit $P=R-C$ expands to

$$P(Q)=-0.5Q^{3}+6Q^{2}+30Q-200$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -1.5Q^{2}+12Q+30
$$

$$
= -1.5(Q-10)(Q+2)
$$

so the only positive critical point is $Q=10$. Marginal revenue is

$$R^{\prime}(Q)=-6Q+90$$

which vanishes at $Q=15$, and $R^{\prime\prime}=-6<0$, so revenue peaks there. Average cost is

$$AC(Q)=0.5Q^{2}-9Q+60+\dfrac{200}{Q}$$

$$AC^{\prime}(Q)=Q-9-\dfrac{200}{Q^{2}}$$

Build time has one-sided slopes $T^{\prime}(Q)=Q+4$ on $Q<12$ and $T^{\prime}(Q)=12$ on $Q\ge 12$. If a rival matches revenue at an endpoint but has strictly larger marginal revenue on an interval, integrating that inequality forces a larger rival revenue at the far end.

tasks.title: Harbour café: drinks, cost, and staffing hours
tasks.context:
A harbour café sells specialty drinks, with daily output $Q$ treated as continuous. Its revenue is $R(Q)=40Q-\dfrac12Q^{2}$ euros and its cost is $C(Q)=\dfrac13Q^{3}-\dfrac92Q^{2}+20Q+80$. During peak service, staffing hours are recorded as
$$H(Q)=\begin{cases}\dfrac12Q^{2}+2Q & \text{if }Q<20\\14Q-120 & \text{if }Q\ge20.\end{cases}$$
Management wants to distinguish a profit condition from a revenue condition and to interpret a competitor's marginal figures correctly. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Profit $R-C$ has a critical point at $Q=10$.
At $Q=8$, marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.
Staffing hours rise more steeply at $Q=18$ than at $Q=24$.
Average cost $\dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}$ is decreasing at $Q=5$.
If a rival café matches this café's revenue at $Q=6$ but has strictly smaller marginal revenue on $6\le Q\le12$, then the rival's revenue at $Q=10$ must be larger than this café's revenue at $Q=10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A critical point of profit is simply a root of $P^{\prime}=0$. Form $P=R-C$, differentiate, and factor — the claim asks only for stationarity, not yet a second-derivative test.

Profit is $P=R-C$. Subtract the given cost from revenue and differentiate.

$$
P(Q) = -\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{3}+4Q^{2}+20Q-80
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -Q^{2}+8Q+20
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -(Q-10)(Q+2)
$$

The factor $Q-10$ shows that $Q=10$ is a stationary point of profit.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Expand output only while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost. Evaluate both derivatives at the named $Q$ and compare them directly.

Compare marginal revenue with marginal cost at the named output.

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 40-Q
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = Q^{2}-9Q+20
$$

At $Q=8$,

$$
R^{\prime}(8) = 32,\qquad C^{\prime}(8)
$$

$$
= 12
$$

Since $32>12$, marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost there.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Staffing steepness is the active branch's derivative. Left of the kink the slope still depends on $Q$; right of it the slope is constant.

Staffing steepness is the derivative on the active branch of $H$.

For $Q<20$,

$$
H^{\prime}(Q) = Q+2
$$

$$
H^{\prime}(18) = 20
$$

For $Q\ge 20$ the slope is constantly $14$, so

$$
H^{\prime}(24) = 14
$$

Because $20>14$, hours rise more steeply at $18$ than at $24$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Average cost is decreasing precisely where $AC^{\prime}<0$. Compute that derivative at $Q=5$ rather than reading the level of $AC$.

Form average cost by dividing, then read the sign of its derivative at $Q=5$.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{1}{3}Q^{2}-\dfrac{9}{2}Q+20+\dfrac{80}{Q}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = \dfrac{2}{3}Q-\dfrac{9}{2}-\dfrac{80}{Q^{2}}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(5) = \dfrac{10}{3}-\dfrac{9}{2}-\dfrac{80}{25}<0
$$

The derivative is negative, so average cost is decreasing at $Q=5$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

A strictly smaller rival marginal revenue accumulates a strictly smaller revenue gain. Equal revenue at the left endpoint then forces a lower rival level at the right.

A rival that matches revenue at $Q=6$ but has strictly smaller marginal revenue on $[6,12]$ accumulates a smaller revenue gain.

$$
R_{e}(10)-R_{e}(6)<R(10)-R(6)
$$

With equal levels at $6$, this forces $R_{e}(10)<R(10)$, not larger. The claim reverses the inequality.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Revenue is $R(Q)=40Q-\dfrac12 Q^{2}$ and cost is $C(Q)=\dfrac13 Q^{3}-\dfrac92 Q^{2}+20Q+80$. Profit $P=R-C$ has

$$P(Q)=-\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{3}+4Q^{2}+20Q-80$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -Q^{2}+8Q+20
$$

$$
= -(Q-10)(Q+2)
$$

so $Q=10$ is a stationary point. The marginal schedules are

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 40-Q,\qquad C^{\prime}(Q)
$$

$$
= Q^{2}-9Q+20
$$

Staffing hours obey $H^{\prime}(Q)=Q+2$ on $Q<20$ and $H^{\prime}(Q)=14$ on $Q\ge 20$. Average cost is

$$AC(Q)=\dfrac{1}{3}Q^{2}-\dfrac{9}{2}Q+20+\dfrac{80}{Q}$$

$$AC^{\prime}(Q)=\dfrac{2}{3}Q-\dfrac{9}{2}-\dfrac{80}{Q^{2}}$$

A rival that matches revenue at an endpoint but has strictly smaller marginal revenue accumulates a smaller revenue gain when that inequality is integrated.

tasks.title: Print shop: price, demand, and elasticity
tasks.context: A print shop faces daily poster demand $D(p)=120-4p$ when price is $p$ euros, where $0<p<30$. Revenue is $R(p)=pD(p)$ and production cost for $Q$ posters is $C(Q)=2Q+0.05Q^{2}$. The owner is considering both the price-side graph and the output-side cost schedule, so a maximum in one representation need not be a profit maximum. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Revenue is maximised at the price $p=15$.
At that revenue-maximising price, the price elasticity of demand equals $-1$.
At the revenue-maximising price, marginal revenue equals marginal cost, so profit is maximised there as well.
If price rises a little from $p=10$, revenue rises.
Average cost $\dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}$ is increasing for every $Q>0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Price-side revenue is $R(p)=p\,D(p)$. Differentiate with respect to $p$, solve $R^{\prime}=0$, and confirm $R^{\prime\prime}<0$ so the critical price is a maximum.

Revenue as a function of price is $R(p)=p(120-4p)$. Differentiate and set the derivative to zero.

$$
R(p) = 120p-4p^{2}
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(p) = 120-8p
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(p) = 0
$$

$$
p = 15
$$

Also $R^{\prime\prime}(p)=-8<0$, so this critical price is a maximum.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Point elasticity is $\varepsilon=\dfrac{D^{\prime}p}{D}$. At a smooth revenue peak the calculus check is unit elasticity — evaluate at the maximising price from A.

Point price elasticity is $\varepsilon=\dfrac{D^{\prime}(p)\,p}{D(p)}$.

$$
\varepsilon(p) = \dfrac{-4p}{120-4p}
$$

At the revenue-maximising price $p=15$,

$$
\varepsilon(15) = \dfrac{-60}{60}
$$

$$
= -1
$$

Elasticity equals $-1$ exactly where revenue peaks.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

A revenue maximum is not a profit maximum. At the revenue peak one has $MR=0$, but profit needs $MR=MC$; check whether marginal cost is also zero there.

At the revenue-maximising price $p=15$, demand is $Q=60$, so marginal revenue is already zero. Marginal cost at that output is

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 2+0.1Q
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(60) = 2+6
$$

$$
2 + 6 = 8
$$

$$
= 8
$$

Since $MR=0\neq 8=MC$, the first-order condition for profit fails there.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

A small price rise raises revenue precisely while $R^{\prime}(p)>0$. Evaluate the price-side derivative at $p=10$ and read its sign.

Ask whether revenue is still rising at $p=10$ by reading the sign of $R^{\prime}$.

$$
R^{\prime}(p) = 120-8p
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(10) = 120-80
$$

$$
120 - 80 = 40
$$

$$
= 40>0
$$

A small price increase from $10$ therefore raises revenue.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Average cost is $C/Q$. After dividing the given quadratic cost, its slope is a positive constant — so $AC$ rises for every positive output.

Average cost is cost per poster.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}
$$

$$
= 2+0.05Q
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = 0.05>0
$$

The derivative is positive for every $Q>0$, so average cost is increasing throughout the positive domain.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Demand is $D(p)=120-4p$ on $0<p<30$, so revenue is

$$R(p)=120p-4p^{2}$$

$$R^{\prime}(p)=120-8p$$

The critical price is $p=15$, and $R^{\prime\prime}=-8<0$, so revenue peaks there. Point elasticity is

$$\varepsilon(p)=\dfrac{-4p}{120-4p}$$

and at $p=15$ one gets $\varepsilon(15)=-1$. Demand at that price is $Q=60$, while

$$C^{\prime}(Q)=2+0.1Q$$

so $C^{\prime}(60)=8$. Average cost is simply $AC(Q)=2+0.05Q$ with $AC^{\prime}(Q)=0.05>0$ for every $Q>0$.

Throughout, distinguish the first-order condition for each objective (profit, revenue, average cost, physical output) and integrate any rival marginal-revenue comparison from a matched endpoint before reading the inequality direction.

tasks.title: Market garden: labour, output, and wage
tasks.context: A market garden sells vegetables for a fixed $2$ euros per kilogram. Output from $L$ labour-hours is $Q(L)=30L-L^{2}$ for $0\le L\le20$, labour costs $12$ euros per hour, and fixed cost is $40$ euros. The grower must compare the value of an extra worker-hour with its wage rather than merely pursue the largest physical harvest. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Profit is maximised at $L=12$ hours.
At that profit-maximising labour input, the value of marginal product equals the wage.
Marginal product of labour is still positive at $L=12$.
Hiring a little more labour than $L=12$ would raise profit.
Output $Q(L)$ itself is maximised at the same labour input that maximises profit.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Profit is revenue from harvest minus the wage bill and fixed cost. Differentiate with respect to labour and solve $\pi^{\prime}=0$; then check $\pi^{\prime\prime}<0$.

Profit is revenue from output minus the wage bill and fixed cost.

$$
\pi(L) = 2(30L-L^{2})-12L-40
$$

$$
= 48L-2L^{2}-40
$$

$$
\pi^{\prime}(L) = 48-4L
$$

$$
\pi^{\prime}(L) = 0
$$

$$
L = 12
$$

Also $\pi^{\prime\prime}=-4<0$, so $L=12$ maximises profit.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

At a labour optimum the value of marginal product equals the wage — that is the economic reading of $\pi^{\prime}=0$. Compute $Q^{\prime}$ and multiply by the output price.

The value of marginal product is price times marginal product of labour.

$$
Q^{\prime}(L) = 30-2L
$$

$$
Q^{\prime}(12) = 30-24
$$

$$
30 - 24 = 6
$$

$$
= 6
$$

$$
VMP = 2\cdot 6
$$

$$
2\times 6 = 12
$$

$$
= 12
$$

That value equals the hourly wage of $12$, which is exactly the profit first-order condition.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Profit can peak while physical output is still rising, because labour is costly. Check the sign of $Q^{\prime}$ at the profit-maximising $L$.

Marginal product at the profit-maximising input is

$$
Q^{\prime}(12) = 30-24
$$

$$
30 - 24 = 6
$$

$$
= 6
$$

The value $6$ is still positive: physical output is still rising, even though the value of that extra kilogram just balances the wage.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Just past a profit maximum the derivative $\pi^{\prime}$ is already negative, so hiring a little more labour lowers profit rather than raising it.

From the profit schedule $\pi(L)=48L-2L^{2}-40$ one has

$$
\pi^{\prime}(L) = 48-4L
$$

which is strictly negative for every $L>12$. Extra labour beyond the critical point therefore reduces profit — that is exactly what a maximum means for the first-order condition.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Physical output peaks where $Q^{\prime}=0$, a different equation from $\pi^{\prime}=0$. Compare that labour input with the profit maximiser.

Physical output is maximised where $Q^{\prime}=0$.

$$
Q^{\prime}(L) = 30-2L
$$

$$
=0
$$

$$
L = 15
$$

That harvest peak at $L=15$ is later than the profit peak at $L=12$, so the two optima do not coincide. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Output is $Q(L)=30L-L^{2}$ sold at $2$ euros per kilogram, with wage $12$ and fixed cost $40$. Profit is

$$
\pi(L) = 2(30L-L^{2})-12L-40
$$

$$
= 48L-2L^{2}-40
$$

$$\pi^{\prime}(L)=48-4L$$

so $\pi^{\prime}=0$ at $L=12$, and $\pi^{\prime\prime}=-4<0$. Marginal product is

$$Q^{\prime}(L)=30-2L$$

hence $Q^{\prime}(12)=6$ and value of marginal product is $VMP=2\cdot 6=12$, matching the wage. Physical output itself peaks where $Q^{\prime}=0$, namely at $L=15$.

Throughout, distinguish the first-order condition for each objective (profit, revenue, average cost, physical output) and integrate any rival marginal-revenue comparison from a matched endpoint before reading the inequality direction.

tasks.title: Courier fleet: routes, cost, and a threshold
tasks.context:
A courier firm operates $x>0$ city routes each day, treated as a continuous planning quantity. Its total operating cost is
$$C(x)=\begin{cases}x^{2}+20x+100&\text{if }x<25\\45x+100&\text{if }x\ge25,\end{cases}$$
while route revenue is $R(x)=60x-\dfrac12x^{2}$. The dispatch manager is testing whether a cost level, its marginal slope, and its average are being confused at the subcontracting threshold. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Marginal cost jumps upward when route volume crosses $x=25$.
For $x<25$, average cost is minimised at $x=10$.
On $x<25$, profit has a critical point at $x=\dfrac{40}{3}$.
At $x=30$, marginal revenue is negative.
Because total cost is continuous at $x=25$, its left- and right-hand derivatives must be equal.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A piecewise cost rule can jump in slope even when the level is continuous. Compare the left- and right-hand derivatives at $x=25$ to see the direction of the jump.

Marginal cost is the derivative of the active cost branch. Approaching the threshold from the left,

$$
C^{\prime}_{-}(x) = 2x+20
$$

$$
C^{\prime}_{-}(25) = 70
$$

On the right branch the slope is constantly $45$, so

$$
C^{\prime}_{+}(25) = 45
$$

The jump is downward from $70$ to $45$, not upward.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

On the first branch, minimise $AC=C/x$ by setting $AC^{\prime}=0$. Solve for the positive critical point and check the sign change of $AC^{\prime}$.

On the first branch, average cost is

$$
AC(x) = x+20+\dfrac{100}{x}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(x) = 1-\dfrac{100}{x^{2}}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(x) = 0
$$

$$
x = 10
$$

The derivative changes from negative to positive at $x=10$, so average cost is minimised there on $x<25$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Restrict profit to the first cost branch, differentiate, and solve $P^{\prime}=0$. That critical point is what the claim names.

On the first cost branch, profit is $P=R-C$.

$$
P(x) = 40x-\dfrac{3}{2}x^{2}-100
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 40-3x
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 0
$$

$$
x = \dfrac{40}{3}
$$

That critical point lies in $x<25$, so the claim matches the calculation.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Marginal revenue is $R^{\prime}$, not the sign of profit. A large route count need not yet put revenue on its downward slope — evaluate the derivative directly from the given revenue rule rather than assuming that “more routes” already means falling revenue.

$$
R(x) = 60x-\dfrac12 x^{2}
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(x) = 60-x
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(30) = 30>0
$$

so marginal revenue is still positive at $x=30$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Continuity of $C$ at the threshold does not force matching one-sided derivatives. Check both the common level and the unequal slopes at $x=25$.

Both cost formulas give the same level at the join,

$$
C(25) = 25^{2}+20\cdot 25+100
$$

$$
= 1225
$$

$$
= 45\cdot 25+100
$$

so $C$ is continuous there. The one-sided slopes are nevertheless $70$ and $45$, which are unequal, so continuity does not force equal derivatives.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Cost is piecewise: $C(x)=x^{2}+20x+100$ for $x<25$ and $C(x)=45x+100$ for $x\ge 25$, with revenue $R(x)=60x-\dfrac12 x^{2}$. One-sided marginal costs at the threshold are

$$
C^{\prime}_{-}(25) = 2\cdot 25+20
$$

$$
= 70,\qquad C^{\prime}_{+}(25)
$$

$$
= 45
$$

while the levels match, $C(25)=1225$, so $C$ is continuous but not differentiable there. On the first branch,

$$
AC(x) = x+20+\dfrac{100}{x},\qquad AC^{\prime}(x)
$$

$$
= 1-\dfrac{100}{x^{2}}
$$

vanishes at $x=10$. Profit on that branch is $P(x)=40x-\dfrac{3}{2}x^{2}-100$, so

$$
P^{\prime}(x) = 40-3x
$$

$$
= 0\implies x
$$

$$
= \dfrac{40}{3}
$$

Marginal revenue is $R^{\prime}(x)=60-x$.

tasks.title: Gift-tube producer: volume, tax, and rival revenue
tasks.context: A gift-tube producer makes cylindrical packages with radius $r$ and height $h=2r$, so package volume is $V(r)=2\pi r^{3}$. Separately, market demand implies price $p(Q)=72-Q$ for $Q$ packages, and a new per-package tax is $6$ euros. The commercial team has mixed a local packaging approximation with output and rival-revenue claims in its report. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Increasing radius from $2$ to approximately $2.02$ changes volume by about $0.48\pi$ cubic units.
The elasticity of package volume with respect to radius is $2$.
Before tax, revenue is maximised at $Q=36$ packages.
After the $6$ euro tax, net revenue is maximised at $Q=30$ packages.
If a rival has the same revenue at $Q=10$ and strictly greater marginal revenue for every output from $10$ to $20$, its revenue at $Q=18$ is greater.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A small radius change is approximated by the differential $\Delta V\approx V^{\prime}(r_{0})\Delta r$. Differentiate the cubic volume rule, then multiply by $\Delta r=0.02$.

Volume is $V(r)=2\pi r^{3}$. Approximate the change by the differential at $r=2$.

$$
V^{\prime}(r) = 6\pi r^{2}
$$

$$
V^{\prime}(2) = 24\pi
$$

With $\Delta r=0.02$,

$$
V^{\prime}(2)\cdot 0.02 = 24\pi\cdot 0.02
$$

$$
= 0.48\pi
$$

The local change in volume is about $0.48\pi$.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Volume elasticity with respect to radius is $\dfrac{r V^{\prime}}{V}$. For $V\propto r^{3}$ the elasticity equals the power $3$, not $2$.

Elasticity of volume with respect to radius is $\dfrac{rV^{\prime}(r)}{V(r)}$.

$$
\dfrac{r}{2\pi r^{3}}\cdot 6\pi r^{2} = 3
$$

The cubic rule in $r$ gives elasticity $3$, not $2$. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim. Carry the derivative comparison all the way to the claimed number before deciding.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Pre-tax revenue is $R(Q)=Q(72-Q)$.

$$
R(Q) = 72Q-Q^{2}
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 72-2Q
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 0
$$

$$
Q = 36
$$

Also $R^{\prime\prime}=-2<0$, so revenue is maximised at $Q=36$ before the tax.

That comparison with the claimed figure is the whole content of the letter. Keep the shared setup's derivative formulas in view throughout.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

A per-package tax lowers net price by $6$, shifting the revenue peak. Solve the new first-order condition — do not reuse the pre-tax critical output.

After a $6$ euro per-package tax, net revenue is $(72-Q-6)Q$.

$$
R_{t}(Q) = 66Q-Q^{2}
$$

$$
R_{t}^{\prime}(Q) = 66-2Q
$$

$$
=0
$$

$$
Q = 33
$$

The critical output is $33$, not $30$. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim. Carry the derivative comparison all the way to the claimed number before deciding.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Equal revenue at $Q=10$ plus a strict rival $MR$ advantage through $Q=18$ integrates to a strictly larger rival revenue at $18$.

Integrate the strict marginal-revenue inequality from $10$ to $18$.

$$
R_{e}(18)-R_{e}(10)>R(18)-R(10)
$$

Equal revenue at $Q=10$ then forces $R_{e}(18)>R(18)$, so the rival finishes higher at $18$.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Riverside market: three-sided stall enclosure
tasks.context: A riverside market builds a rectangular stall enclosure using the river as one long side, so only three sides of fencing are needed. Eliminate the river-parallel side from the fencing budget and substitute into area $A=xy$. Record the open interval where both sides stay positive.

The fencing constraint is $2x+y=120$, so eliminate $y$.

$$
y = 120-2x
$$

$$
A(x) = x(120-2x)
$$

$$
= 120x-2x^{2}
$$

The open interval $0<x<60$ is exactly where both $x$ and $y$ stay positive.

**B.** → True

Maximise the resulting quadratic area on that open interval. Solve $A^{\prime}=0$ and confirm $A^{\prime\prime}<0$ so the critical width is a maximum.

Differentiate the reduced area and set the derivative to zero.

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 120-4x
$$

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 0
$$

$$
x = 30
$$

Also $A^{\prime\prime}=-4<0$, so area is maximised at $x=30$ metres.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

At the area-maximising width, recover the parallel length from the fencing constraint rather than guessing a convenient number from the diagram of the stall.

The first-order condition

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 120-4x
$$

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 0
$$

$$
y = 120-2\cdot 30
$$

$$
= 60
$$

metres along the river — exactly the length named in the claim. That is the river-parallel side of the enclosure.

**D.** → False

The second-derivative test fails only when $A^{\prime\prime}=0$ at the critical point. Here $A^{\prime\prime}$ is a negative constant, so the test succeeds.

The second derivative at the critical point is

R^{\prime}(Q) = 0
$$

$$
Q = 6
$$

Also $R^{\prime\prime}=-6<0$, so revenue is maximised at $Q=6$ batches.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Invert demand to $Q(p)$, then evaluate point elasticity at the revenue-maximising output's price. A smooth revenue peak forces $\varepsilon=-1$.

Demand is $Q=\dfrac{36-p}{3}$, so $D^{\prime}(p)=-\dfrac{1}{3}$. At $Q=6$ one has $p=18$, and

$$
\varepsilon = \dfrac{D^{\prime}(p)\cdot p}{Q}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\cdot 18}{6}
$$

$$
= -1
$$

Elasticity equals $-1$ at the revenue-maximising output.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

With constant unit cost, profit is $R-6Q$. Its critical point solves $P^{\prime}=0$, which is not the same root as $R^{\prime}=0$.

With unit cost $6$, profit is $P=R-6Q$.

P(Q) = 30Q-3Q^{2}
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = 30-6Q
$$

$$
=0

$$
Q = 5

Profit peaks at $Q=5$, not at the revenue maximum $Q=6$. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim. Carry the derivative comparison all the way to the claimed number before deciding.

**D.** → True

Marginal revenue is the derivative of revenue with respect to batches. Expand $R(Q)=p(Q)\,Q$ under inverse demand $p=36-3Q$, differentiate term by term, then evaluate at the named output:

R(Q) = 36Q-3Q^{2}

R^{\prime}(Q) = 36-6Q
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(4) = 36-24

$$
36 - 24 = 12

$$
= 12

exactly the marginal revenue the claim reports. Do not confuse this positive $MR$ with the revenue peak at $Q=6$.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

A falling price does not force falling revenue while $MR>0$. On $(0,6)$ one has $R^{\prime}>0$, so revenue is still rising despite a declining price.

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 36-6Q>0\quad\text{on }(0,6)
$$

Revenue is still increasing on that interval. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim.

tasks.solution_overview:
Inverse demand $p=36-3Q$ gives revenue

$$R(Q)=36Q-3Q^{2}$$

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = 36-6Q
$$

= 0\implies Q

= 6

with $R^{\prime\prime}=-6<0$. At that output $p=18$, and demand $Q=\dfrac{36-p}{3}$ has point elasticity $-1$. tasks.title: Founder's wealth utility: risk attitude
tasks.context: A founder evaluates wealth $w$ (in thousands of euros) with utility $U(w)=20w-0.05w^{2}$ on $0<w<200$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Marginal utility is positive throughout $0<w<200$.
The founder is risk-averse on this interval because $U^{\prime\prime}(w)<0$.
Utility itself is maximised at $w=200$.
At $w=50$, marginal utility equals $15$.
A mean-preserving spread of wealth around $w=80$ would raise expected utility.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Marginal utility is $U^{\prime}$. Differentiate the given quadratic utility and check whether $U^{\prime}$ stays positive on the whole open interval $(0,200)$.

Marginal utility is the first derivative of $U$.

$$
U^{\prime}(w) = 20-0.1w
$$

On the open interval $0<w<200$ one has $0.1w<20$, so $U^{\prime}(w)>0$ throughout.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Risk aversion is the calculus signature $U^{\prime\prime}<0$ (strict concavity). Compute the second derivative and read its sign on the interval.

Risk aversion for a smooth utility is the statement that the second derivative is negative.

$$
U^{\prime\prime}(w) = -0.1<0
$$

Utility is strictly concave on the interval, which is the usual calculus signature of risk aversion.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Setting $U^{\prime}=0$ hits the right endpoint $w=200$, which is not an interior point of $(0,200)$. On the open interval utility is still strictly increasing.

Setting $U^{\prime}=0$ gives $w=200$, which is the right endpoint of the open interval. On $(0,200)$ one still has $U^{\prime}>0$, so utility is strictly increasing and has no interior maximum below $200$. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Marginal utility is the first derivative of the given quadratic utility. Differentiate term by term, then evaluate at the named wealth level rather than reading the utility level $U(50)$ itself:

$$
U(w) = 20w-0.05w^{2}
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(w) = 20-0.1w
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(50) = 20-5
$$

$$
20 - 5 = 15
$$

$$
= 15
$$

exactly as claimed. The utility level $U(50)$ itself is a different quantity from this slope. Slope and level are different objects here.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

For a strictly concave $U$, Jensen's inequality goes the other way: a mean-preserving spread lowers expected utility rather than raising it.

Because $U$ is strictly concave, Jensen's inequality runs the other way: a mean-preserving spread around $w=80$ lowers expected utility rather than raising it. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim. Carry the derivative comparison all the way to the claimed number before deciding.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Utility is $U(w)=20w-0.05w^{2}$ on $0<w<200$. Marginal utility and its derivative are

$$
U^{\prime}(w) = 20-0.1w,\qquad U^{\prime\prime}(w)
$$

$$
= -0.1
$$

On the open interval $0.1w<20$, so $U^{\prime}>0$ throughout, while $U^{\prime\prime}<0$ means strict concavity (risk aversion). Setting $U^{\prime}=0$ would give the right endpoint $w=200$, which is not an interior maximum on $(0,200)$. At $w=50$, $U^{\prime}(50)=15$. Strict concavity implies that a mean-preserving spread lowers expected utility by Jensen's inequality.

tasks.title: Design duo: two inputs under a budget
tasks.context: A design duo spends a budget of $M=40$ euros on hours of illustration $x$ and hours of typesetting $y$, with prices $p_{x}=2$ and $p_{y}=4$, so $2x+4y=40$. Creative output is $U(x,y)=xy$. Reduce the problem to one free variable and treat it as an ordinary single-variable optimisation. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Eliminating $y$ gives $U(x)=10x-\dfrac12 x^{2}$ for $0<x<20$.
Output is maximised at $x=10$ illustration hours.
At that point the duo buys $y=5$ typesetting hours.
At the optimum one has $\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{p_{y}}{p_{x}}$.
Spending the entire budget on illustration alone ($y=0$) maximises $U$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Solve the budget for typesetting hours and substitute into $U=xy$. Record the open interval where both inputs stay positive.

Solve the budget $2x+4y=40$ for typesetting hours and substitute into $U=xy$.

$$
y = 10-\dfrac{1}{2}x
$$

$$
U(x) = x\left(10-\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)
$$

$$
= 10x-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}
$$

The reduced function on $0<x<20$ matches the claim.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Maximise the reduced single-variable objective. Solve $U^{\prime}=0$ and confirm $U^{\prime\prime}<0$ so the critical illustration hours maximise output.

Differentiate the reduced output and set the derivative to zero.

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 10-x
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 0
$$

$$
x = 10
$$

Also $U^{\prime\prime}=-1<0$, so output is maximised at $10$ illustration hours.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

At the optimum illustration hours, recover typesetting hours from the budget relation rather than from a separate first-order condition on $y$.

The reduced objective had

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 10-x
$$

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 0
$$

 at $x=10$. Substituting into $y=10-\dfrac12 x$ recovers

$$
y = 10-\dfrac12\cdot 10
$$

$$
= 5
$$

typesetting hours — the complementary purchase forced by the budget at that optimum. The corner $y=0$ is not needed for this letter.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

The MRS–price condition equates $y/x$ to $p_{x}/p_{y}$, not to the reciprocal $p_{y}/p_{x}$. Check which ratio actually holds at the interior optimum.

At the interior optimum one has $\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The price ratio in the MRS condition is

$$
\dfrac{p_{x}}{p_{y}} = \dfrac{2}{4}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

not $\dfrac{p_{y}}{p_{x}}=2$. The claim writes the reciprocal ratio.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

Spending the whole budget on illustration forces $y=0$ and $U=xy=0$. Compare that corner with the interior maximum value.

Spending the entire budget on illustration alone forces $y=0$, hence

$$
U(x,0) = 0
$$

The interior maximum is $U(10,5)=50$, far above that corner of zero. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim. Carry the derivative comparison all the way to the claimed number before deciding.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The budget $2x+4y=40$ gives $y=10-\dfrac12 x$. Creative output $U=xy$ then reduces to

$$U(x)=10x-\dfrac12 x^{2}$$

on $0<x<20$. Differentiating yields

$$
U^{\prime}(x) = 10-x
$$

$$
= 0\implies x
$$

$$
= 10
$$

with $U^{\prime\prime}=-1<0$, and the corresponding typesetting hours are $y=5$. At that point $\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac12=\dfrac{p_{x}}{p_{y}}$, matching the MRS–price condition (not the reciprocal $\dfrac{p_{y}}{p_{x}}$). The corner $y=0$ forces $U=0$, far below the interior maximum $U(10,5)=50$.

Throughout, distinguish the first-order condition for each objective (profit, revenue, average cost, physical output) and integrate any rival marginal-revenue comparison from a matched endpoint before reading the inequality direction.

tasks.title: Bike workshop: cubic P′ and a per-unit levy
tasks.context: A bike workshop's weekly profit $P(Q)$ is not printed as a formula. The figure shows only marginal profit $P^{\prime}(Q)$, with zeros marked at $Q=1$, $Q=4$ and $Q=9$. Later the city proposes a per-unit levy that would shift the entire $P^{\prime}$ graph down by a constant $6$ units (same shape, lower by $6$). Use the figure and that proposed shift. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: On the open interval $(4,9)$, the workshop should expand a little: $P^{\prime}>0$ there.
Profit has a local maximum at $Q=4$ and a local minimum at $Q=9$.
Among the three marked zeros, the global maximiser of $P$ on $[0,11]$ must be $Q=9$ if $P(0)=0$ and $P$ only changes through $P^{\prime}$.
After the levy shifts $P^{\prime}$ down by $6$, the old zero at $Q=4$ is no longer a zero of the new marginal profit.
Reading the scale near $Q=6$, pre-levy $P^{\prime}$ exceeds $15$, so even after the $6$-unit levy the workshop would still want to expand at $Q=6$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The figure plots marginal profit $P^{\prime}$, with zeros at $Q=1$, $4$, and $9$. Read the sign of $P^{\prime}$ on the open interval $(4,9)$ from the cubic's position relative to the axis.

Marginal profit sits above the axis wherever a little more output raises profit. Between the zeros at $4$ and $9$ the cubic factorisation keeps $P^{\prime}$ positive, so

$$
P^{\prime}(Q)>0\quad\text{on }(4,9)
$$

The workshop should expand a little on that open interval.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

Local max/min of $P$ follow the sign changes of $P^{\prime}$. A $-$ to $+$ flip is a local minimum; a $+$ to $-$ flip is a local maximum — check which occurs at $4$ and at $9$.

Reading the sign chart of $P^{\prime}$: positive on $(0,1)$, negative on $(1,4)$, positive on $(4,9)$, and negative after $9$. A change from $-$ to $+$ at $Q=4$ marks a local minimum, and a change from $+$ to $-$ at $Q=9$ marks a local maximum — the reverse of the claim.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → False

A local maximum need not be the global maximiser on $[0,11]$. Without comparing profit levels at critical points and endpoints, the figure alone does not force $Q=9$ to be global.

A local maximum at $Q=9$ need not be the global maximiser on $[0,11]$. Without comparing profit levels at $Q=1$, at $Q=9$, and at the endpoints, the figure alone does not force $Q=9$ to be the global max.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

A per-unit levy shifts the entire $P^{\prime}$ graph down by $6$. At the old zero $Q=4$ the pre-levy height was $0$, so after the shift the new height is $-6\neq 0$. That abscissa is therefore no longer a zero of the post-levy marginal profit. That comparison with the claimed figure is the whole content of the letter. Keep the shared setup's derivative formulas in view throughout.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Read the pre-levy height of $P^{\prime}$ near $Q=6$ from the factored cubic. Subtract $6$ and check whether the post-levy marginal profit is still positive.

Near $Q=6$, reading the factored cubic,

$$
P^{\prime}(6) = -(6-1)(6-4)(6-9)
$$

$$
= -(5)(2)(-3)
$$

$$
= 30
$$

After the levy subtracts $6$ one still has $24>0$, and $30$ already exceeds $15$, so expansion remains profitable at $Q=6$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: The figure shows a cubic marginal-profit curve with zeros at $Q=1$, $Q=4$, and $Q=9$. The sign chart of $P^{\prime}$ is positive on $(0,1)$, negative on $(1,4)$, positive on $(4,9)$, and negative after $9$. Consequently $Q=4$ is a local minimum (sign change $-$ to $+$) and $Q=9$ is a local maximum ($+$ to $-$). A local maximum need not be the global maximiser on $[0,11]$ without comparing profit levels at the critical points and endpoints. A per-unit levy shifts the entire $P^{\prime}$ graph down by $6$, so every old zero moves: at the old zero $Q=4$ the new height is $-6\neq 0$. Near $Q=6$, reading the factored cubic gives $P^{\prime}(6)=30$, which still exceeds $15$ and remains positive after subtracting $6$.

tasks.title: Candle maker: curved MC against MR, with AC* trap
tasks.context: A candle maker plots marginal revenue (brown), marginal cost (green), and the variable part of average cost $AC^{*}$ (purple) on one plane. The marked intersection of brown and green is at $Q=8$. No algebraic formulas are printed — reason from the figure and standard optimisation logic. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: At outputs a little below $Q=8$, brown lies above green, so expanding output raises profit.
Profit is maximised where purple meets brown, because that is where average cost equals marginal revenue.
At $Q=12$, green lies above brown, so a little less output would raise profit.
Because green is convex and rising through the brown line from below, the brown–green crossing is a local profit maximum.
The height of the brown–green crossing equals maximised total profit $P(8)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Profit rises wherever $MR>MC$. Just left of the marked brown–green crossing, read which curve lies above the other and translate that into a profit direction.

Profit rises wherever marginal revenue lies above marginal cost. Just left of the brown–green crossing at $Q=8$, the brown MR curve sits above the green MC curve, so $MR>MC$ and expanding output raises profit.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

An interior profit maximum requires brown meeting green ($MR=MC$). Purple meeting brown would be $AC^{*}=MR$, a different and generally wrong locus.

The profit first-order condition equates marginal revenue with marginal cost — brown meeting green. Purple meeting brown is where the variable average-cost schedule crosses MR, which is a different and generally wrong locus for maximising profit.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Profit falls wherever marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, so the figure's ordering of green and brown at a named output decides whether to expand or cut.

At $Q=12$ the figure has green (MC) above brown (MR), hence

$$
MR<MC
$$

and cutting output a little raises profit there — the mirror image of the expansion region left of the brown–green crossing at $Q=8$. Read the curves, not a guessed formula.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

Because green is convex and rising through falling brown from below, $MR-MC$ changes from $+$ to $-$ at the crossing — the local signature of a profit maximum.

Because green MC is convex and rising through the falling brown MR line from below, the difference $MR-MC$ changes from positive to negative at the crossing. That sign change is the signature of a local profit maximum.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

The height of the brown–green crossing is the common marginal value $MR=MC$ at $Q=8$. Total maximised profit $P(8)$ is an accumulated stock, not that single marginal height. The intermediate algebra above contradicts the claim. That mismatch with the claimed figure is the whole content of the letter. Keep the shared setup's derivative formulas in view throughout.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The figure plots marginal revenue (brown), marginal cost (green), and the variable part of average cost $AC^{*}$ (purple), with the brown–green crossing marked at $Q=8$. Profit rises wherever $MR>MC$ and falls wherever $MR<MC$, so the first-order condition for a local profit maximum is the brown–green crossing — not a purple–brown meeting of $AC^{*}$ with MR. Because green is convex and rising through the falling brown line from below, $MR-MC$ changes from positive to negative at $Q=8$, confirming a local profit maximum. The height of that crossing is the common marginal value $MR=MC$ at $Q=8$; total maximised profit $P(8)$ is an accumulated stock, not that single marginal height.

tasks.title: Clinic throughput: f, f′ and f″ on one plane
tasks.context: A clinic tracks a throughput index $f$ (brown), its derivative $f^{\prime}$ (green), and its second derivative $f^{\prime\prime}$ (purple) on one shared figure. Throughput is measured against a staffing intensity $x$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Brown has a local minimum near $x=1$ and a local maximum near $x=5$.
Purple crosses zero near $x=3$, and that is an inflection of brown: concavity of $f$ changes there.
Where purple is negative (right of $x=3$), green is decreasing — matching $f^{\prime\prime}=(f^{\prime})^{\prime}$.
The highest point of green is a local maximum of brown.
At $x=3$, brown is climbing, green is positive, and purple is near zero — so staffing intensity $3$ maximises throughput itself.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Brown is the throughput level $f$, and green is its slope $f^{\prime}$. Local extrema of brown therefore sit where green crosses the axis and changes sign — not where green merely peaks.

Near $x=1$, green passes from negative to positive, so the slope of throughput flips from downhill to uphill: brown bottoms out there — a local minimum.

Near $x=5$, green passes from positive to negative, so the climb of brown turns into a descent: brown peaks there — a local maximum.

Those two turning points are exactly the ones named in the claim.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Purple is $f^{\prime\prime}$, the concavity meter for brown. An inflection of $f$ is a zero of $f^{\prime\prime}$ where that second derivative changes sign — a flip of concavity, not a peak of the level itself.

The figure shows purple crossing through zero near $x=3$, switching from positive to negative. Left of that crossing brown is concave up; right of it brown is concave down.

So staffing intensity near $3$ is precisely an inflection of throughput $f$, which is what the claim asserts.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

By definition $f^{\prime\prime}=(f^{\prime})^{\prime}$, so the sign of purple is exactly the slope of green: purple positive means green is rising, purple negative means green is falling.

Wherever purple lies below the axis — which the figure shows for $x$ right of $3$ — green must be decreasing. That is not an extra geometric accident; it is the chain of derivatives written in colours.

The claim records exactly that consistency between the two derivative curves.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

The highest point of green is where $f^{\prime}$ itself is largest — the steepest climb of brown — not a turning point of brown. At that staffing intensity, throughput is still rising as fast as it ever does.

A local maximum of brown requires green to cross through zero with a $+$ to $-$ sign change, which happens near $x=5$, well after green's peak.

The claim confuses a peak of the slope with a peak of the level.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → False

At $x=3$, purple is near zero (an inflection of brown), while green is still positive, so the slope of throughput is still uphill: brown is climbing, not peaking.

The staffing intensity that maximises throughput itself is where green crosses down through zero, near $x=5$. An inflection with a still-positive first derivative is a change of concavity, not a maximum of $f$.

The claim treats the inflection as a throughput maximum.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure stacks three related curves against staffing intensity $x$: brown is the throughput level $f$, green is its slope $f^{\prime}$, and purple is $f^{\prime\prime}$.

Local extrema of brown sit where green crosses the axis and changes sign: near $x=1$ green flips $-$ to $+$, so brown has a local minimum; near $x=5$ green flips $+$ to $-$, so brown has a local maximum.

An inflection of brown is a zero of purple with a sign change. Purple crosses through zero near $x=3$ (from $+$ to $-$), so $f$ changes from concave up to concave down there.

By definition $f^{\prime\prime}=(f^{\prime})^{\prime}$, so wherever purple is negative (right of $x=3$), green must be decreasing. The peak of green is only the steepest climb of brown — not a turning point of brown — and at the inflection $x=3$ green is still positive, so throughput is still rising toward its maximum near $x=5$.

tasks.title: Ceramic kiln: cost inflection and marginal cost
tasks.context: A ceramic kiln has weekly cost $C(Q)=Q^{3}-6Q^{2}+40Q+10$ for output $Q\ge0$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Marginal cost is $C^{\prime}(Q)=3Q^{2}-12Q+40$.
$C$ has an inflection point at $Q=2$.
On $(0,2)$, marginal cost is decreasing.
Average cost equals marginal cost at every inflection point of $C$.
At $Q=0$, fixed cost is $10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Marginal cost is the derivative of weekly total cost with respect to output. Differentiate the cubic term by term, using the power rule on each monomial.

$$
C(Q) = Q^{3}-6Q^{2}+40Q+10
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 3Q^{2}-12Q+40
$$

Do not confuse this derivative with average cost $C(Q)/Q$; marginal cost is the instantaneous rate of change of total cost, not the per-chair average.

There is no need to simplify further: that quadratic is already the claimed schedule. Matching the expression to the claim.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

An inflection of total cost is a zero of $C^{\prime\prime}$ where that second derivative changes sign. Differentiate the marginal-cost quadratic once more.

$$
C^{\prime\prime}(Q) = 6Q-12
$$

$$
6Q-12 = 0\qquad
$$

$$
\qquad Q
$$

$$
= 2
$$

The trap would be stopping at $C^{\prime\prime}(2)=0$ without checking the sign change; here the flip from negative to positive confirms a genuine inflection.

On $(0,2)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}<0$ (concave down), and on $(2,\infty)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}>0$ (concave up). Concavity of $C$ therefore flips at $Q=2$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Marginal cost falls precisely where its own derivative is negative — that is, where $C^{\prime\prime}<0$. From the second derivative already obtained,

$$
C^{\prime\prime}(Q) = 6Q-12
$$

$$
= 6(Q-2)
$$

Past $Q=2$ the second derivative turns positive, so marginal cost begins to rise — the interval $(0,2)$ is exactly the falling-MC region.

On the open interval $(0,2)$ one has $Q-2<0$, so $C^{\prime\prime}<0$ strictly. Therefore $C^{\prime}$ is decreasing throughout $(0,2)$, which is exactly the claim.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

An inflection of total cost is the condition $C^{\prime\prime}=0$ with a sign change. Equality of average and marginal cost is a different equation: it is the first-order condition for a critical point of $AC=\dfrac{C}{Q}$, coming from the quotient rule.

Those two algebraic conditions need not share the same root. At the inflection $Q=2$ there is no requirement that $AC=MC$ — confusing an inflection of $C$ with a critical point of $AC$ is the trap.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Fixed cost is the cost of producing nothing — the value of the cost function at zero output, before any variable kiln runs.

$$
C(0) = 0-0+0+10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
0 + 0 = 0
$$

$$
0 + 10 = 10
$$

$$
= 10
$$

Variable cost starts from zero at $Q=0$, so the entire $C(0)$ reading is fixed cost; nothing in the cubic's higher-degree terms contributes at the origin.

That matches the constant term in the cubic cost rule, and it is precisely the fixed-cost reading the claim asserts.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Weekly kiln cost is the cubic

$$C(Q)=Q^{3}-6Q^{2}+40Q+10\qquad(Q\ge 0)$$

Differentiate once for marginal cost and once more for concavity:

$$C^{\prime}(Q)=3Q^{2}-12Q+40$$

$$C^{\prime\prime}(Q)=6Q-12$$

$$
C^{\prime\prime}(Q) = 0\implies Q
$$

$$
= 2
$$

On $(0,2)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}<0$, so $C$ is concave down and $C^{\prime}$ is decreasing; on $(2,\infty)$ one has $C^{\prime\prime}>0$, so $C$ is concave up. Thus $Q=2$ is an inflection of $C$ and the place where marginal cost stops falling.

Fixed cost is the level at zero output: $C(0)=10$. Equality $AC=MC$ is the different first-order condition for a critical point of $AC=C/Q$; it need not hold at the inflection $Q=2$.

tasks.title: Pop-up shop: Newton quotient for weekend profit
tasks.context: A pop-up shop models weekend profit (hundreds of euros) by $P(x)=x^{2}-6x+20$, where $x$ is the number of staffed hours. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: The Newton quotient $\dfrac{P(a+h)-P(a)}{h}$ simplifies to $2a+h-6$.
The tangent line at $x=4$ is $y=2x$.
Profit is decreasing for all $x>3$.
$x=3$ is a local minimum of $P$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The Newton quotient is the average slope of profit between $a$ and $a+h$. Expand the shifted value, cancel $P(a)$, and divide by $h$.

$$
P(a+h) = (a+h)^{2}-6(a+h)+20
$$

$$
= a^{2}+2ah+h^{2}-6a-6h+20

tasks.title: App studio: square-root learning cost
tasks.context: An app studio's cumulative production cost for $Q>0$ releases is $C(Q)=80\sqrt{Q}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Marginal cost is $C^{\prime}(Q)=\dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}$.
Average cost is decreasing for every $Q>0$.
Marginal cost equals half of average cost at every $Q>0$.
Doubling cumulative output doubles total cost.
At $Q=16$, marginal cost equals $10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Rewrite the square-root cost as a power and apply the power rule carefully.

$$
C(Q) = 80Q^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 80\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
= 40Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

As $Q$ grows, this marginal cost falls — each extra release costs less than the previous one — which is the learning-curve content of the square-root rule.

That is the claimed marginal-cost schedule: each extra release costs $40$ divided by the square root of cumulative output. Matching the expression to the claim.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Average cost is total cost per release. Divide, then differentiate with the power rule.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{80\sqrt{Q}}{Q}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
= 80Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = 80\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}
$$

$$
= -40Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}
$$

A falling AC does not require falling total cost; here $C$ itself still rises because $MC>0$, while the average is pulled down by spreading the early expensive releases.

For every $Q>0$ this derivative is strictly negative, so average cost is decreasing throughout the positive domain.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Compare the two closed forms side by side — both are constant over $\sqrt{Q}$.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}},\qquad MC(Q)
$$

$$
= \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
\dfrac{MC}{AC} = \dfrac{40}{80}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

This half-relationship is special to the square-root (homogeneous of degree $1/2$) technology; it is not a general AC–MC identity.

So $MC=\dfrac{1}{2}AC$ at every $Q>0$, not just at a special output. That half-relationship is exactly the claim.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

Scaling cumulative output by $2$ scales a square-root cost by $\sqrt{2}$, not by $2$. The trap is treating $C$ as linear in $Q$.

$$
C(2Q) = 80\sqrt{2Q}
$$

$$
= \sqrt{2}\cdot 80\sqrt{Q}
$$

$$
= \sqrt{2}\,C(Q)
$$

Under linear cost, doubling output would double cost; under $C\propto\sqrt{Q}$ the scale factor is only the square root of two.

Total cost rises by the factor $\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41$, not by a factor of $2$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Evaluate the marginal-cost formula at the named output, taking the positive square root.

$$
C^{\prime}(16) = \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{16}}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{40}{4}
$$

$$
= 10
$$

Equivalently, $MC(16)=\tfrac12 AC(16)$ and $AC(16)=80/4=20$, so $MC=10$ again — the same numerical check.

Equivalently, $MC(16)=\tfrac12 AC(16)$ and $AC(16)=80/4=20$, so half of average cost is again $10$ — a second numerical check of the same formula.

So at sixteen releases the cost of one more release is $10$, matching the claim exactly.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Cumulative production cost is the square-root rule

$$
C(Q) = 80\sqrt{Q}
$$

$$
= 80Q^{\frac{1}{2}}\qquad(Q>0)
$$

Power-rule differentiation and the average-cost quotient give

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = MC(Q)
$$

$$
= \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{Q}}
$$

$$AC^{\prime}(Q)=-40Q^{-\frac{3}{2}}<0\qquad(Q>0)$$

so average cost falls throughout. Comparing the closed forms, $MC=\dfrac{1}{2}AC$ at every $Q>0$. Scaling output by two scales cost by $\sqrt{2}$ only: $C(2Q)=\sqrt{2}\,C(Q)$. At $Q=16$,

$$
C^{\prime}(16) = \dfrac{40}{4}
$$

$$
= 10
$$

tasks.title: Coffee subscription: MU against a constant opportunity cost
tasks.context: A coffee subscription models a subscriber's marginal utility of cups $c$ per month (brown). Each cup also has a constant opportunity cost of $6$ utility units, so the green curve is $\mathrm{MU}-6$. Interior cups are worthwhile while green is positive. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Without the opportunity cost, utility of cups would keep rising until about $c=45$.
Accounting for the opportunity cost, the subscriber's best cup count among the plotted options is near $c=30$, where green crosses zero.
At $c=10$, green lies above height $10$.
Because brown is linear and falling, utility $U(c)$ is strictly concave on this range.
Green lying below brown by a constant means the optimal cup count is where brown itself is maximised.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Without the opportunity cost, cups remain worthwhile while marginal utility itself stays positive — that is, while brown lies above the axis.

Brown crosses zero near $c=45$, so $\mathrm{MU}>0$ on $(0,45)$ and the subscriber's utility of cups keeps rising until about that count. Beyond $45$, brown is negative and additional cups would lower utility.

The claim records exactly that zero of brown as the stop rule when opportunity cost is ignored.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

With a constant opportunity cost of $6$, an extra cup is worthwhile only while $\mathrm{MU}-6>0$, i.e. while green is positive. The stop rule is green crossing zero:

$$
\mathrm{MU} = 6
$$

Do not stop where brown itself is largest or where brown hits zero; with opportunity cost present, the relevant crossing is green $=0$.

Green crosses zero near $c=30$ on the figure. Among the plotted options that is the best cup count — not the later zero of brown near $45$, which ignores the opportunity cost.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Read the heights at $c=10$ carefully. Brown (marginal utility) sits at height $14$ there, and green is the parallel shift $\mathrm{MU}-6$.

$$
14-6 = 8
$$

If one mistakenly read brown's height $14$ as green's height, the claim would look true — subtracting the constant $6$ is the step that falsifies it.

Height $8$ lies below $10$, not above it. The trap is misreading brown's height as green's, or forgetting to subtract the constant $6$.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Utility $U$ has derivative $\mathrm{MU}$ (brown). A linear falling brown curve means $U^{\prime}$ has constant negative slope, so the second derivative is a negative constant:

$$
U^{\prime\prime} = (\mathrm{MU})^{\prime}<0
$$

Linear falling MU is the strongest form of diminishing marginal utility on this window: the second derivative never approaches zero. throughout the plotted range. Strict negativity of $U^{\prime\prime}$ is exactly strict concavity of $U$ on this range.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Green is a parallel downward shift of brown by the constant $6$. The optimal cup count solves green $=0$, i.e. $\mathrm{MU}=6$ — an equality of marginal utility with opportunity cost.

Brown itself is linear and falling on the whole window, so it has no interior maximum at all. The stop rule is the zero of green, not a peak of brown; confusing the two curves' roles is the trap.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure plots a subscriber's marginal utility of cups $c$ (brown) together with the opportunity-cost gap

$$\mathrm{green}=\mathrm{MU}-6$$

a parallel downward shift of brown by the constant $6$. Interior cups remain worthwhile while green is positive.

Brown (MU) stays positive until it crosses the axis near $c=45$, so without the opportunity cost, utility of cups keeps rising until about that count. Green crosses zero near $c=30$, which is the stop rule $\mathrm{MU}=6$ and the best cup count among the plotted options.

At $c=10$, brown sits at height $14$, so green sits at $14-6=8$ (below height $10$). Because brown is linear and falling, $U^{\prime\prime}=(\mathrm{MU})^{\prime}<0$ throughout, so $U$ is strictly concave. Brown itself has no interior maximum on the window; the optimum is the zero of green, not a peak of brown.

tasks.title: Cold-chain: spoilage index over delivery hours
tasks.context: A cold-chain delivery records a spoilage index $S(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$ over $0\le t\le4$ hours after loading. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Spoilage has a local maximum at $t=1$.
Spoilage has a local minimum at $t=3$.
Among the critical points in $(0,4)$, the global maximum of $S$ on $[0,4]$ is at $t=1$.
$S^{\prime\prime}(1)<0$ and $S^{\prime\prime}(3)>0$, matching the local max / local min reading.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Differentiate the spoilage index term by term, then factor the resulting quadratic.

$$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2}-12t+9
$$

$$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3(t^{2}-4t+3)
$$

$$
= 3(t-1)(t-3)
$$

The roots $t=1$ and $t=3$ of this factorisation are the only interior candidates for local extrema of spoilage on $(0,4)$.

The claimed factorisation matches exactly, and the roots $t=1$ and $t=3$ will drive the later local-extremum reading. Matching the expression to the claim.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Classify $t=1$ by the sign chart of $S^{\prime}=3(t-1)(t-3)$.

For $t\in(0,1)$ both factors are negative, so the product is positive and $S^{\prime}>0$. Between $1$ and $3$ the factor $(t-1)$ is positive while $(t-3)$ is negative, so $S^{\prime}<0$.

Equivalently,

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = 6\cdot 1-12
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = -6<0
$$

 confirms the same local-max reading by the second-derivative test.

A $+$ to $-$ change at $t=1$ is a local maximum of spoilage.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Continue the same sign chart past $t=3$.

On $(1,3)$ one has $S^{\prime}<0$, and for $t>3$ both factors $(t-1)$ and $(t-3)$ are positive, so $S^{\prime}>0$.

Equivalently,

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 6\cdot 3-12
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 6>0
$$

 confirms the same local-min reading by the second-derivative test.

A $-$ to $+$ change at $t=3$ is a local minimum of spoilage — spoilage falls into a trough there before rising again toward the right endpoint.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

A local maximum among critical points need not be the unique global maximum on a closed interval. Compare levels at the endpoints and at every critical point.

$$
S(0) = 0,\qquad S(1)
$$

$$
= 1-6+9
$$

$$
= 4,\qquad S(3)
$$

$$
= 27-54+27
$$

$$
= 0,\qquad S(4)
$$

$$
= 64-96+36
$$

$$
= 4
$$

On a closed interval the global maximum can sit at an endpoint even when an interior local max exists; here the endpoint $t=4$ ties the local peak.

Both $t=1$ and $t=4$ attain height $4$, so the global maximum on $[0,4]$ is not uniquely at $t=1$.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

The second-derivative test should match the local max / local min reading already obtained from the sign chart.

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(t) = 6t-12
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(1) = 6-12
$$

$$
6 - 12 = -6
$$

$$
= -6<0
$$

$$
S^{\prime\prime}(3) = 18-12
$$

$$
18 - 12 = 6
$$

$$
= 6>0
$$

The second-derivative test and the first-derivative sign chart are two readings of the same geometry; agreement between them is what the claim records.

Negative second derivative at $t=1$ confirms a local max, and positive second derivative at $t=3$ confirms a local min — exactly the claimed match.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Spoilage over $0\le t\le 4$ is

$$S(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$$

Differentiating and factoring,

$$
S^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2}-12t+9
$$

$$
= 3(t-1)(t-3)
$$

$$S^{\prime\prime}(t)=6t-12$$

Sign chart of $S^{\prime}$: positive on $(0,1)$, negative on $(1,3)$, positive on $(3,4)$. So $t=1$ is a local maximum and $t=3$ is a local minimum, matching $S^{\prime\prime}(1)=-6<0$ and $S^{\prime\prime}(3)=6>0$.

Closed-interval levels: $S(0)=0$, $S(1)=4$, $S(3)=0$, $S(4)=4$. Both $t=1$ and $t=4$ attain the global maximum height $4$ on $[0,4]$, so that maximum is not unique to $t=1$.

tasks.title: Two workshops: compare P′ graphs and levels
tasks.context: Two neighbouring workshops $A$ (brown) and $B$ (green) plot marginal profit on one plane. Both start with $P_A(0)=P_B(0)=0$. Use the figure. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Workshop $A$ has a local profit maximum at $Q=6$.
Workshop $B$ still has positive marginal profit at $Q=6$, so $B$ would expand past $A$'s stationary output.
Because both start at profit $0$ and brown lies above green on $(0,6)$, it follows that $P_A(6)>P_B(6)$.
On $(6,9)$, workshop $A$ should contract while workshop $B$ should expand.
The height where brown meets green (near $Q=3$) is the profit level $P_A(3)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Workshop $A$'s marginal profit is the brown curve. A local profit maximum occurs where brown crosses from positive to negative: that is where the first-order condition $P_A^{\prime}=0$ holds with a $+$ to $-$ sign change.

That crossing sits at $Q=6$ on the figure. Left of $6$, brown is positive so $A$'s profit is rising; right of $6$, brown is negative so profit is falling.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Workshop $B$'s marginal profit is green. At $Q=6$, green still lies above the axis — it only reaches zero near $Q=9$.

Workshop $A$ has already hit $P_A^{\prime}=0$ at $Q=6$, while $B$ still has $P_B^{\prime}>0$ there — the two workshops' stationary outputs need not coincide.

Positive marginal profit means $B$'s total profit is still rising at the output where $A$ has already stopped. So $B$ would expand past $A$'s stationary output, which is exactly the comparison in the claim.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Both workshops start at profit zero. On $(0,6)$ brown lies above green, so $P_A^{\prime}>P_B^{\prime}$ throughout that interval. Integrating the strict inequality from the common start yields

$$
P_A(6)-P_A(0)>P_B(6)-P_B(0)
$$

and with $P_A(0)=P_B(0)=0$ one obtains $P_A(6)>P_B(6)$. The trap would be comparing heights of the $P^{\prime}$ curves at a single point instead of integrating the gap.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

On $(6,9)$ brown lies below the axis while green still lies above it.

The interval $(6,9)$ is exactly the stretch where the two workshops' first-order advice diverges: $A$ wants less output, $B$ wants more.

Negative marginal profit tells workshop $A$ to contract (reduce $Q$); positive marginal profit tells workshop $B$ to expand (increase $Q$). Those are exactly the opposite directions named in the claim.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Where brown meets green near $Q=3$, the two workshops share a common marginal-profit value:

$$
P_A^{\prime}(3) = P_B^{\prime}(3)
$$

Profit levels are areas under the $P^{\prime}$ curves from $0$; a single shared height of the derivative graphs does not equal either workshop's accumulated profit.

That shared height is a value of the derivatives, not a level of total profit. In particular it is not $P_A(3)$ — confusing the ordinate of a $P^{\prime}$ graph with a profit level is the trap.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Workshops $A$ (brown) and $B$ (green) plot marginal profit $P_A^{\prime}$ and $P_B^{\prime}$, both starting from

$$
P_A(0) = P_B(0)
$$

$$
= 0
$$

Brown crosses from positive to negative at $Q=6$, so $A$ has a local profit maximum there. At that same $Q=6$, green is still positive (zero only near $Q=9$), so $B$'s profit is still rising and $B$ would expand past $A$'s stationary output.

On $(0,6)$ brown lies above green, so $P_A^{\prime}>P_B^{\prime}$. Integrating from the common zero start yields $P_A(6)>P_B(6)$.

On $(6,9)$ brown is negative while green remains positive, so $A$ should contract and $B$ should expand. Where brown meets green (near $Q=3$), the shared height is a common marginal-profit value $P_A^{\prime}=P_B^{\prime}$, not the profit level $P_A(3)$.

60 - 30 = 30
$$

$$
D(15) = 30
$$

, then $R=pD=450$, matching the marked figure point.

Equivalently, from the line $D=60-2p$ one computes

$$
D(15) = 60-30
$$

$$
60 - 30 = 30
$$

$$
D(15) = 30
$$

, then $R=pD=450$, matching the marked figure point without further differentiation.

That is the revenue at the named price — no elasticity or cost calculation is needed for this letter.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

The figure's line is the linear demand $D=60-2p$, with slope $D^{\prime}=-2$. Point elasticity is

$$
\varepsilon(p) = \dfrac{D^{\prime}(p)\,p}{D(p)}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{-2p}{60-2p}
$$

At $p=15$,

$$
\varepsilon = \dfrac{-2\cdot 15}{60-30}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{-30}{30}
$$

$$
= -1
$$

For linear demand, unit elasticity is also the revenue-maximising price:

$$
R^{\prime}(15) = 60-4\cdot 15
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(15) = 0
$$

, so the elasticity reading and the revenue FOC agree.

Unit elasticity holds at that price, which is also where revenue peaks for linear demand.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → False

Unit elasticity maximises revenue ($MR=0$), not profit. At $p=15$ one has $Q=30$, and marginal cost is

$$
C^{\prime}(Q) = 4+\dfrac{Q}{10}
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(30) = 4+3
$$

$$
4 + 3 = 7
$$

$$
= 7\neq 0
$$

A firm that stops at the revenue peak ignores the still-positive marginal cost of printing those thirty posters; profit keeps the cost side in the FOC.

Profit maximisation requires $MR=MC$. Here $MR=0$ while $MC=7$, so $p=15$ is a revenue peak but not a profit maximum — that is the classic trap.

So the statement is False.
**D.** → True

Read demand at $p=10$ from the figure, then evaluate marginal cost and the revenue derivative.

$$
D(10) = 60-20
$$

$$
60 - 20 = 40
$$

$$
= 40
$$

$$
C^{\prime}(40) = 4+\dfrac{40}{10}
$$

$$
= 8
$$

All three pieces of the claim — demand $40$, $MC=8$, and $R^{\prime}(10)>0$ — are verified by direct substitution into the figure line and the cost rule.

With $R(p)=60p-2p^{2}$, one has $R^{\prime}(p)=60-4p$, so $R^{\prime}(10)=20>0$: a small price increase from $10$ still raises revenue.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → True

Form average cost by dividing total cost by output, then differentiate.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q}
$$

$$
= 4+\dfrac{Q}{20}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = \dfrac{1}{20}>0
$$

Unlike a U-shaped average-cost curve with a positive fixed-cost term, this cost rule has no fixed cost, so $AC$ starts at $4$ and drifts upward linearly.

The derivative is a positive constant, so average cost is strictly increasing for every $Q>0$ — there is no U-shaped dip for this quadratic cost.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure's demand line is $D(p)=60-2p$, and production cost is

$$C(Q)=4Q+\dfrac{1}{20}Q^{2}$$

$$C^{\prime}(Q)=4+\dfrac{Q}{10}$$

$$
AC(Q) = 4+\dfrac{Q}{20},\qquad AC^{\prime}(Q)
$$

$$
= \dfrac{1}{20}>0
$$

so average cost rises for every $Q>0$. Revenue $R(p)=p(60-2p)$ has $R^{\prime}(p)=60-4p$. At $p=15$, demand is $D(15)=30$, so $R=450$, and elasticity is $\varepsilon=\dfrac{-2p}{60-2p}=-1$.

Unit elasticity maximises revenue ($MR=0$), but at $Q=30$ one has $C^{\prime}(30)=7\neq 0$, so $p=15$ is not a profit maximum. At $p=10$, demand is $40$, $C^{\prime}(40)=8$, and $R^{\prime}(10)=20>0$.

tasks.title: Spice importer: per-unit tax shifts MC on the figure
tasks.context: A spice importer's MR (brown) and MC (green) are shown, together with post-tax marginal cost (purple) after a specific tax of $4$ per unit. Pre-tax they meet near $Q=16$; post-tax purple meets brown nearer $Q=\dfrac{40}{3}$. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Pre-tax, expanding a little from $Q=12$ raises profit because brown is above green there.
The tax raises the profit-maximising output.
Post-tax, at the new crossing the firm equates MR to MC plus the tax.
At $Q=20$, even pre-tax, green already exceeds brown, so that output is past the pre-tax optimum.
Because purple is a parallel upward shift of green by $4$, every post-tax optimum output must satisfy $MR=MC$ with the old green curve.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Profit rises while marginal revenue lies above marginal cost, and falls once MC overtakes MR. On the figure, at $Q=12$ brown (MR) still sits above green (MC), left of their pre-tax crossing near $Q=16$.

The pre-tax optimum is the later green–brown crossing near $Q=16$; at $Q=12$ one is still in the region where expanding raises profit.

Expanding a little from that output therefore adds more to revenue than to cost, raising pre-tax profit.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → False

A specific tax of $4$ shifts marginal cost upward to the purple curve. The new $MR=\mathrm{MC}+\mathrm{tax}$ crossing is the purple–brown meeting near $Q=\dfrac{40}{3}$.

A higher per-unit cost schedule intersects the unchanged MR curve farther left, so optimal output contracts — the standard comparative-static of a specific tax.

That abscissa lies left of the pre-tax green–brown crossing near $Q=16$, so the tax lowers optimal output rather than raising it. The trap is thinking a cost shock expands production.

So the statement is False.
**C.** → True

Purple is the post-tax marginal cost — the old MC plus the tax of $4$ per unit. Where purple meets brown, the firm equates marginal revenue to that shifted cost schedule:

$$
MR = \mathrm{MC}+\mathrm{tax}
$$

In symbols, if green is $MC(Q)$ then purple is $MC(Q)+4$, and the post-tax stationary point solves $MR(Q)=MC(Q)+4$.

That is precisely the post-tax first-order condition, not a coincidence of the drawing.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → True

The pre-tax optimum is the green–brown crossing near $Q=16$. At $Q=20$, which lies to the right of that crossing, green already exceeds brown: $MC>MR$.

Put differently: past the pre-tax FOC, the firm is on the wrong side of $MR=MC$, so cutting output toward $16$ would raise pre-tax profit.

Marginal cost above marginal revenue means each extra unit loses money, so that output is past the pre-tax optimum.

So the statement is True.
**E.** → False

Purple is a parallel upward shift of green by $4$, so the post-tax first-order condition uses purple, not the old green curve.

The parallel shift changes the intercept of MC but not its slope; what matters for the FOC is that the firm faces purple, not green, after the tax.

Equivalently the firm solves $MR=\mathrm{MC}+4$, not $MR=\mathrm{MC}$. Keeping the untaxed green FOC would locate the wrong output — that is the trap of ignoring the tax in the FOC.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure shows pre-tax MR (brown) and MC (green), together with post-tax marginal cost (purple) after a specific tax of $4$ per unit — a parallel upward shift of green by $4$.

Pre-tax, brown meets green near $Q=16$. At $Q=12$ brown still lies above green, so expanding a little raises pre-tax profit. At $Q=20$, past that crossing, green already exceeds brown, so output is past the pre-tax optimum.

Post-tax, purple meets brown nearer $Q=\dfrac{40}{3}<16$. The new first-order condition is $MR=\mathrm{MC}+\mathrm{tax}$, so the tax lowers optimal output rather than raising it. Keeping the untaxed condition $MR=\mathrm{MC}$ with the old green curve would be wrong — the firm must use purple.

tasks.title: Herb box: inverse demand inside a fencing budget
tasks.context: A market gardener fences a three-sided herb bed with $2x+y=60$ metres of fence (river on one side) and sells the harvest under inverse demand $p=24-\dfrac{1}{2}A$ where $A=xy$ is planted area. Revenue is $R=pA$. Treat $A$ as the quantity index. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Eliminating $y$ gives planted area $A(x)=60x-2x^{2}$ for $0<x<30$.
Area alone (ignoring price response) is maximised at $x=15$.
Revenue $R(A)=24A-\dfrac12 A^{2}$ is maximised at $A=24$.
The area-maximising fence layout automatically maximises revenue, because $A=15\cdot30=450$ exceeds $24$.
At the revenue-maximising area $A=24$, price elasticity of demand equals $-1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Eliminate the parallel side from the fencing budget and write planted area in the free length $x$.

$$
y = 60-2x
$$

$$
A(x) = x\cdot y
$$

$$
= x(60-2x)
$$

$$
= 60x-2x^{2}
$$

The factor $2$ in $2x$ comes from the two equal sides perpendicular to the river; the river itself supplies the fourth side for free.

The open fencing interval requires $y>0$ and $x>0$, so $0<x<30$, exactly as claimed. Matching the reduced area rule to the claim.

So the statement is True.
**B.** → True

Maximise the concave quadratic area on that open interval, ignoring price response for this letter.

$$
A^{\prime}(x) = 60-4x
$$

$$
60-4x = 0\qquad
$$

$$
\qquad x
$$

$$
= 15
$$

$$
A^{\prime\prime}(x) = -4<0
$$

At $x=15$ one has

$$
y = 60-30
$$

$$
60 - 30 = 30
$$

$$
y = 30
$$

 and planted area

$$
A = 15\cdot 30
$$

$$
15\times 30 = 450
$$

$$
A = 450
$$

, the largest rectangle the fence budget can enclose.

This letter maximises physical area alone; price response and revenue enter only in later letters.

So area alone is maximised at $x=15$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Revenue as a function of planted area is the quadratic coming from inverse demand $p=24-\dfrac{1}{2}A$.

$$
R(A) = pA
$$

$$
= \left(24-\dfrac{1}{2}A\right)A
$$

$$
= 24A-\dfrac{1}{2}A^{2}
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(A) = 24-A
$$

$$
24-A = 0\qquad
$$

$$
\qquad A
$$

$$
= 24
$$

This is a pure revenue calculation treating $A$ as the quantity index; the fencing constraint is set aside until one asks whether $A=24$ is feasible (it is).

And $R^{\prime\prime}=-1<0$, so revenue peaks at $A=24$.

So the statement is True.
**D.** → False

The area-maximising layout gives a huge planted area:

$$
A(15) = 60\cdot 15-2\cdot 15^{2}
$$

$$
= 900-450
$$

$$
= 450
$$

Feasibility is not the issue — $A=450$ is attainable — but revenue at $A=450$ is dragged down by the low price

$$
p = 24-\frac12\cdot 450
$$

$$
p = -201
$$

, which is economically absurd on this demand line.

Revenue, however, peaks at $A=24$, far below $450$. Flooding the market with area drives price down along the inverse-demand line; maximising physical area is not the same as maximising revenue.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

Invert the demand rule to express quantity in terms of price, then evaluate elasticity at the revenue-maximising area.

$$
p = 24-\dfrac{1}{2}A\qquad
$$

$$
\qquad A
$$

$$
= 48-2p
$$

At $A=24$ one has $p=12$, so

\varepsilon = \dfrac{-2p}{48-2p}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{-2\cdot 12}{48-24}
$$

$$
= \dfrac{-24}{24}
$$

$$
= -1
$$

For linear inverse demand, unit elasticity always marks the revenue peak:

$$
R^{\prime}(A) = 24-A
$$

$$
R^{\prime}(A) = 0
$$

 at the same $A=24$ where $\varepsilon=-1$.

Unit elasticity at the revenue peak is exactly what the claim asserts.

Three-sided fencing $2x+y=60$ gives $y=60-2x$ and planted area

R^{\prime}(A) = 24-A
$$

$$
= 0\implies A
$$

$$
= 24
